r-p6-01:1.why: L yes ('them' reads fine locally if 'the stairs' is taken as antecedent; 'one' also fits 'leave __ free'). D yes (the antecedent 'the elevator that remains in service' is in the previous sentence). r-p6-01:1.editorNote: 'one' is not defensible: the antecedent is a single, definite elevator (only one remains in service), so 'one' (= an elevator) would imply a second one is available. 'them' needs a plural antecedent: the only plural noun is 'the stairs', which contradicts the instruction to use them. 'theirs' has no possessor. Good pronoun trap, no change needed.

B failed: no one actively believes 'has been' (a standing arrangement) because the clause says 'normally used only by building staff'. S failed: the timeline check is trivial.
r-p6-01:2.editorNote: 'has been open ... each weekday' would claim the freight elevator is already open to tenants, which clashes with 'normally used only by building staff' and with an e-mail about work starting a week later. Not defensible. Past forms are plainly out.

r-p6-01:3.editorNote: 'even if' (postpone large deliveries even when the dock can take them) contradicts the whole point of opening the freight elevator for deliveries in paragraph 2. 'because' and 'although' give the wrong logical relation. No ambiguity.

B failed: 'Nevertheless' needs a negative in the previous sentence and none exists, so it is not strongly believed. S failed.
r-p6-02:0.editorNote: 'Nevertheless' would require a drawback in the trial results; the previous sentence reports only a benefit. 'Otherwise' and 'For example' do not fit the relation. No ambiguity.

r-p6-02:1.editorNote: 'no longer' nearly survives: it contradicts 'Our auditors may ask to see them' only if 'them' means the original receipts; a reader could take 'them' to be the photographed copies and read the last sentence as a neutral remark. I judge the original-receipts reading the natural one ('them' is the nearest plural, 'the original receipts'), so I do not mark it ambiguous. 'not yet' and 'already' make no sense.

D contradicts paragraph 1 (Tallyway replaces the paper forms on October 1). Minor and not an answer issue: 'must be submitted by the 5th' is a little strong when late claims are still paid the next month; 'need to be submitted' would be smoother.

r-p6-02:3.fix: To lift it to medium, push the main verb away: 'Claims {4} after the 5th, even by a single day, will be repaid the following month instead.'
r-p6-02:3.editorNote: 'submitting', 'submit' and 'are submitted' are all clearly wrong in the full sentence. This is the one easy item in the file; it is within the 'at most one easy per passage' limit.

r-p6-03:1.why: L yes ('will begin in March' and 'began in March' are both fine in the sentence, and 'will begin' pairs naturally with 'due to open in October'). D yes (the dateline June 12 and 'this autumn' are in paragraph 1). B yes ('will begin' for a plan-style news story; 'has begun' as the news present perfect). S yes (work out that March is before June 12, so the work has already started, and that 'will begin in March' would clash with an opening this October). No letter failed.
r-p6-03:1.editorNote: 'has begun in March' (present perfect with a definite past time) and 'had begun in March' (no past reference point in the sentence) would be changed by an editor. 'will begin in March' contradicts the June 12 dateline plus 'this autumn'. No ambiguity. Good time-reference item.

r-p6-03:2.why: L yes ('Once' reads naturally in the sentence). D yes (the previous sentence, 'take over all of Corvell's pastry production', decides). B yes ('Once ... is running at full capacity' is the most typical temporal frame). S yes (combine 'all' with 'however' and 'will continue' to see that the pastry baking at Mill Road is a temporary arrangement). No letter failed.
r-p6-03:2.fix: Remove the capacity loophole in the previous sentence, e.g. 'The new site has room for all of Corvell's pastry production, leaving Mill Road to concentrate on bread.' Then 'Once the new site is running at full capacity, ... Mill Road will continue to bake some pastries' contradicts the passage outright.
r-p6-03:2.editorNote: Closest call in the file. 'Once the new site is running at full capacity, however, Mill Road will continue to bake some pastries' can be read as 'even at full capacity the new site cannot take every pastry', which fits the contrastive 'however' and 'full capacity'. It still contradicts 'take over all' and 'leaving Mill Road to concentrate on bread', so I do not mark it ambiguous, but it needs the outside assumption that the new site is too small. 'Even though' and 'In case' do not fit.

r-p6-03:3.editorNote: 'obligation' and 'necessity' are also odd collocations with 'be given'. No ambiguity.

overall: No mustFix: in all 16 questions I found exactly one answer that holds in standard formal written English across the whole document. Answers: r-p6-01 C A B D; r-p6-02 D B A C; r-p6-03 B D C A; r-p6-04 A C D B. Bands by 8.3: 1 easy (r-p6-02:3), 7 medium, 8 hard, so easy is about 6% and hard exactly 50%, on target for round 7. Per passage: r-p6-01 has only one hard question (8.1 wants at least two); the other three have two or three. Each passage has exactly one sentence-insertion blank and 2-3 word blanks, and the body text is 155-196 words including headers, inside the 120-200 range. The insertion items are the strongest: in every case the wrong sentence is the natural continuation of the preceding sentence and is only killed by the following sentence or a later paragraph (r-p6-01:0 A, r-p6-02:2 C, r-p6-03:0 A, r-p6-04:1 A). The passages read like real business documents; dates, prices and names are consistent (March 16 is a Monday in 2026, five days March 16-20, $96 to $72 plus $30 print option, 'this autumn' with an October opening and March start). Compared with the official Part 6 sample, the set leans on discourse logic (connectors, tense by dateline, insertions) and has few plain part-of-speech or collocation blanks; that fits the 'harder' request but is a different mix from the sample, whose first blank is usually a quick part-of-speech item. Style notes: the letter in r-p6-04 has no addressee or salutation, and r-p6-03 repeats 'however' in an option and in the text of the same paragraph group. Items judged borderline easy within medium: r-p6-01:3 and r-p6-03:3 (the collocation gives 'opportunity' away).
